title: Options I: mechanics, the four positions, and the T-chart

reading.h: Opening, closing, and the two count words
reading.body:
Every option order ticket is marked as one of four things. An **opening purchase** starts a new long (buy to open). An **opening sale** starts a new short (write to open). A **closing sale** ends a long you already own (sell to close). A **closing purchase** buys back a short you wrote (buy to close).

Two counts ride on top of these. **Volume** is the number of contracts traded in a day. **Open interest** is the number of contracts still outstanding, meaning opened but not yet closed, exercised, or expired. Opening trades raise open interest; closing trades lower it.

A position ends in one of three ways. It **expires**, it is **closed out** (most common), or it is **exercised or assigned**.

reading.h: The clocks: expiration, last trade, exercise cutoff
reading.body:
Standard monthly equity options **expire on the third Friday** of the expiration month, at **11:59 p.m. ET**. But **trading stops at 4:00 p.m. ET** on that Friday.

The customer's decision to exercise must reach the broker by **5:30 p.m. ET** on expiration day. Firms may set earlier internal deadlines.

Anything left over goes to **exercise by exception (automatic exercise)**. The OCC exercises any equity option that is **$0.01 or more in the money** at expiration, unless the holder files contrary instructions.

**LEAPS** (Long-term Equity AnticiPation Securities) are long-dated options, good for up to **39 months** (the exam says "up to 3 years"). Everything else about them works the same.

reading.h: The four single positions as P&L
reading.body:
Burn the four into memory again, now as P&L you can picture on a price line.

**Long call** — bullish. Loss capped at the premium. Gain unlimited above the breakeven. **BE = strike + premium**.

**Short (naked) call** — bearish or neutral. Gain capped at the premium. Loss **unlimited** above the breakeven. **BE = strike + premium**.

**Long put** — bearish. Loss capped at the premium. Gain grows as the stock falls toward zero, maxing at **strike − premium**. **BE = strike − premium**.

**Short (naked) put** — bullish or neutral. Gain capped at the premium. Loss grows as the stock falls, maxing at **strike − premium**. **BE = strike − premium**.

The buyer and writer of the same contract share the same breakeven. One is the mirror image of the other.

reading.h: The T-chart: the tool that solves everything
reading.body:
You do not memorize P&L formulas for multi-leg positions. You build a **T-chart**. Draw a capital T. The **left** column is **Debit, money out**. The **right** column is **Credit, money in**. Enter every leg per share.

Premiums you pay go on the left; premiums you receive go on the right. When you assume exercise, the stock you buy (at the strike) goes left, and the stock you sell goes right. Then net the two columns, and multiply by 100 (and by the number of contracts) to get dollars.

**Breakeven** is the stock price that makes the two columns equal. Take a long 50 call @ 4: you paid 4 (left). To get it back, you need 4 of intrinsic value, which happens at a stock price of 54. That is the breakeven. The T-chart makes the bookkeeping plain so you never lose a leg.

reading.h: Worked single legs with the T-chart
reading.body:
**Short 1 ABC Jun 50 call @ 4, stock rises to 70, assigned.** You must deliver stock. You buy it in the market at 70 (Out: 70) and sell it at the strike 50 (In: 50). You collected the 4 premium (In: 4). Out 70, In 54, so net −16 × 100 = **−$1,600**. There is no ceiling. The naked call is the unlimited-risk position.

**Long 1 XYZ Sep 40 put @ 3, stock falls to 30, exercise.** You buy stock at 30 (Out: 30) and sell it at the strike 40 through the put (In: 40). You paid the 3 premium (Out: 3). Out 33, In 40, so net +7 × 100 = **+$700**.

**Short 1 XYZ Sep 40 put @ 3, stock falls to 30, assigned.** You are forced to buy at 40 (Out: 40) stock now worth 30 (In: 30). You keep the 3 (In: 3). Out 40, In 33, so **−$700**. This mirrors the long put's gain.

The premium of any option splits into two parts. **Intrinsic value** is how much it is in the money, and it is never below zero. **Time value** is everything else, what buyers pay for the chance of a bigger move before expiration.

**Time value = premium − intrinsic value.**

Say ABC trades at 58 and an ABC Mar 50 call is quoted at 10. Intrinsic value = 58 − 50 = 8. Time value = 10 − 8 = **2**.

As expiration nears, time value decays toward zero. So at expiration an option is worth only its intrinsic value. Deep-in-the-money and expiring options trade near **parity**, meaning intrinsic value only.

The exam keeps asking which position has unlimited risk. The honest answer: only a position exposed to a rising stock price with no cap.

Among single positions, that is **only the naked short call**. You may have to deliver stock you do not own at any price. A long put's loss is capped at the premium. A short put's loss is capped at strike − premium, because a stock stops at zero. A long call's loss is the premium.

Hold onto the rule: the only thing with no ceiling is a stock price. So unlimited risk means being short a call or short the stock itself. Everything else is bounded.

flashcards.back: Open interest = contracts still outstanding (not closed/exercised/expired). Volume = contracts traded that day. Opening raises OI; closing lowers it.
Opening purchase (buy to open long), opening sale (write to open short), closing sale (sell a long), closing purchase (buy back a short).
Monthly equity options expire the 3rd Friday at 11:59 p.m. ET; trading stops 4:00 p.m. ET that day.
Decision to broker by 5:30 p.m. ET on expiration day; OCC auto-exercises anything $0.01 or more ITM.
Up to 39 months (exam: "up to 3 years"). Otherwise ordinary options.
Left = Debit / money out (premiums paid, stock bought at strike). Right = Credit / money in (premiums received, stock sold). Net × 100.
Time value = premium − intrinsic value. At expiration, time value = 0, so premium = intrinsic value (parity).

flashcards.front: ABC 58, 50 call @ 10: intrinsic and time value?
Short call written 50 @ 4, stock to 70: loss?
flashcards.back: Buy 70, sell 50, keep 4 → −16 × 100 = −$1,600, uncapped. Naked call = unlimited risk.

flashcards.front: Which single positions have unlimited loss?
flashcards.back: Only the naked short call (and short stock). A stock price is the only thing with no ceiling.

quiz.stem: A customer buys 1 ABC Jun 50 call at 4. What is the breakeven point at expiration?
quiz.explanation: Calls ADD: breakeven = strike + premium = 50 + 4 = 54, the same for buyer and writer. "46" applies the put rule (subtract), "50" forgets the premium, and "58" double-counts it.

quiz.stem: A customer writes 1 XYZ Sep 40 put at 3. What is the maximum potential loss?
quiz.explanation: If XYZ goes to zero the writer must buy worthless stock at 40, offset by the 3 collected: (40 − 3) × 100 = $3,700. "$300" is the max GAIN, "$37" forgets the ×100, and "$4,300" flips the sign by adding the premium.

quiz.stem: A customer writes 1 ABC Jun 50 call at 4. At expiration ABC is trading at 70 and the call is exercised against the customer. Ignoring commissions, what is the result?
quiz.explanation: T-chart: buy the stock to deliver at 70 (out), sell it at the strike 50 (in), keep the 4 premium (in). 50 + 4 − 70 = −16 × 100 = $1,600 loss. "$2,000" ignores the premium; the gain answers get the direction backward — a naked call assigned above the strike loses.

quiz.stem: ABC stock trades at 58. An ABC Mar 50 call is quoted at 10. What is the time value of the call?
quiz.explanation: Intrinsic value = stock − strike = 58 − 50 = 8; time value = premium − intrinsic = 10 − 8 = 2. "8" is the intrinsic value and "10" is the whole premium.

quiz.stem: A customer buys 1 XYZ Sep 40 put at 3. At expiration XYZ is 30 and the customer exercises. Ignoring commissions, the profit or loss is:
quiz.explanation: Buy stock at 30, sell at the 40 strike via the put, less the 3 premium: (40 − 30 − 3) × 100 = $700 profit. "$1,000" forgets the premium, "$1,300" adds it instead of subtracting, and "$300 loss" is the result only if the put had expired.

quiz.stem: On the third Friday of the expiration month, an equity option holder wanting to exercise must get the decision to the broker no later than:
options: 11:59 p.m. ET, when the option expires
quiz.explanation: The exercise-decision cutoff is 5:30 p.m. ET on expiration day. Trading stops at 4:00 p.m. ET and the contract does not expire until 11:59 p.m. ET, but a holder who wants to exercise (rather than rely on the $0.01 auto-exercise) must instruct the broker by 5:30.

quiz.stem: The number of option contracts that have been opened but not yet closed, exercised, or expired is called:
quiz.explanation: Open interest counts outstanding contracts; it rises with opening transactions and falls with closing ones. Volume is the day's trades, and position/exercise limits cap how many contracts a customer may hold or exercise — different concepts.

quiz.stem: Which of the following positions carries UNLIMITED potential loss?
quiz.explanation: Only the naked short call is unlimited: the writer may have to deliver stock at any price as it rises without ceiling. A long call risks only the premium, a long put only the premium, and a short put at most strike − premium (a stock stops at zero).
